procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 20.01.2023 of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad in A482 No. 11426 of 2021
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The CBI filed a petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. before the High Court at Allahabad, assailing the Magistrate's discharge order dated 31.08.2019. The petition was registered as Application U/S 482 No. 11426 of 2021. The High Court allowed the CBI's petition, effectively overturning the discharge order.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants (who were discharged by the Magistrate) appealed the High Court's order to the Supreme Court via Criminal Appeal No. 1980 of 2024. The Supreme Court is considering whether the High Court could convert or treat a petition filed under section 482 Cr.P.C., as one filed under section 397 Cr.P.C.

directions: The criminal appeal is allowed accordingly.
Order of the High court is set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether it is open for High Court to convert or treat a petition filed under section 482 Cr.P.C., as one filed under section 397 Cr.P.C.

facts: A Special Magistrate discharged the appellants from criminal charges.
The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), aggrieved by the discharge order, had the option to file a revision petition under Section 397 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.).
The limitation period for filing such a revision is 90 days.
The CBI did not file a revision within the 90-day period. Instead, nearly one and a half years later, it filed a petition before the High Court under its inherent powers in Section 482 Cr.P.C.
The High Court entertained the petition and set aside the discharge order.
The appellants challenged the High Court's order before the Supreme Court, arguing that the petition under Section 482 was not maintainable.
law: Section 397 Cr.P.C. provides a specific statutory remedy of revision against orders like the one of discharge.
Article 131 of the Limitation Act, 1963, prescribes a 90-day time limit for filing a criminal revision.
Section 482 Cr.P.C. grants the High Court inherent powers, for which there is no prescribed limitation period.
The inherent power under Section 482 should ordinarily not be exercised when there is an express and specific remedy available under the Code, such as a revision under Section 397.
A revision petition (S. 397) found to be not maintainable can be treated by the High Court as a petition under its inherent powers (S. 482) to secure the ends of justice.

However, the reverse is not necessarily true; a petition filed under Section 482 cannot be blindly converted or treated as a revision under Section 397, especially without considering other issues like the statutory limitation period.
application: The Supreme Court found that the CBI had a specific and adequate remedy available to it by way of a revision petition under Section 397 Cr.P.C.
The Court noted that the CBI chose to ignore this remedy and instead filed a petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. long after the 90-day limitation period for a revision had expired.
The Court concluded that the CBI's action was a clear attempt to circumvent the mandatory limitation period prescribed for filing a revision.
Applying the legal principle that inherent powers should not be a substitute for a specific remedy, the Court held that the CBI should not have been allowed to resort to Section 482.

The Court explicitly rejected the idea that a High Court could simply treat the Section 482 petition as a Section 397 revision. It reasoned that such a conversion would ignore critical issues, most importantly the fact that the petition was filed well beyond the statutory time limit for a revision.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that it is not open for a High Court to convert or treat a petition filed under Section 482 Cr.P.C. as one filed under Section 397 Cr.P.C. The Court held that when a specific remedy of revision under Section 397 is available, it cannot be bypassed by invoking the High Court's inherent powers under Section 482, especially to overcome the statutory limitation period. Therefore, the High Court erred in entertaining the CBI's petition.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the order of discharge passed by the Trial Court.

facts: The Trial Court (Special Judicial Magistrate) discharged the appellants of charges under Sections 420 (cheating) and 120B (criminal conspiracy) IPC, exercising its power under Section 239 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.).
The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) challenged this discharge order by filing a petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. before the High Court.

The High Court set aside the Trial Court's discharge order. It reasoned that the appellants had deliberately withheld relevant information (that the land was encumbered) to deceitfully obtain approvals for setting up educational institutions.
The appellants then appealed the High Court's decision to the Supreme Court.
law: Section 239 Cr.P.C.: Allows a Magistrate to discharge an accused if, after considering the police report and documents, the Magistrate considers the charge against the accused to be groundless.
Section 120A IPC (Criminal Conspiracy): Requires an agreement between two or more persons to do an illegal act or a legal act by illegal means.
Section 420 IPC (Cheating): Requires proving that the accused dishonestly induced a person to deliver property or consent to the retention of property. A key element is deceitful inducement.
application: The Supreme Court analyzed the merits of the case and disagreed with the High Court's reasoning.
It found that the High Court's conclusion that the appellants deliberately withheld information was "not supported by the admitted facts."
The Supreme Court noted that the facts actually showed a "disclosure of the mortgage at the outset when the first application was made."
Because of this initial disclosure, the Supreme Court held that there was "no possibility of inferring that the appellants conspired... to commit an illegal act of suppression."

Furthermore, the Court pointed out that a crucial element for the charge of cheating was missing: the approving authority (AICTE) never claimed that it was dishonestly induced to grant the approvals. Without this essential link, the charge of cheating could not be sustained.
The Supreme Court characterized the High Court's approach as "rather technical" and concluded that the Magistrate was correct in finding the charges to be groundless.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Trial Court (Magistrate) was fully justified in discharging the appellants, as the facts did not support the charges of cheating or criminal conspiracy. It found that the High Court erred in setting aside the discharge. Therefore, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and restored the Trial Court's order discharging the appellants.

cases.principle: Inherent jurisdiction cannot be exercised to nullify the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. Where the Code expressly deals with a particular matter, that provision should normally be regarded as exhaustive.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a specific remedy, such as an appeal or revision, is provided by the Code of Criminal Procedure or the Code of Civil Procedure, the court's inherent power under Section 482 CrPC or Section 151 CPC cannot and should not be resorted to.
obiter: The inherent powers of the court are complementary to the powers specifically conferred by the Code and cannot be exercised in a manner contrary to or different from the procedure expressly provided.
Inherent jurisdiction cannot be exercised to nullify the express provisions of the Code.
Where the Code deals expressly with a particular matter, that provision should normally be regarded as exhaustive.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court erred both procedurally and on the merits. Procedurally, it was not open for the High Court to entertain a petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. when the specific statutory remedy of a revision under Section 397 Cr.P.C. was available to the CBI. On the merits, the High Court's finding that the appellants deliberately withheld information was factually incorrect, as records showed disclosure of the bank loan, and the essential element of dishonest inducement was not met because the allegedly induced party (AICTE) never made such a complaint.
legal_tests_applied: When there is a specific remedy provided by way of appeal or revision the inherent power under Section 482 CrPC or Section 151 CPC cannot and should not be resorted to.

Inherent jurisdiction cannot be exercised so as to nullify the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Where the Code deals expressly with a particular matter, the provision should normally be regarded as exhaustive.
why_appellant_lost: Not applicable as the appellant's appeal was allowed by the Supreme Court.
why_respondent_won: The CBI improperly ignored the specific statutory remedy available to it under Section 397 Cr.P.C and instead resorted to filing an application under Section 482 Cr.P.C., which was not permissible.

The High Court's finding of deliberate withholding of information was factually incorrect, as it was a 'matter of record that the first application dated 22.01.2007 filed by appellant No. 1 on behalf of the Society disclosed that a bank loan was still outstanding'.

The element of dishonest inducement was not established, as the only party who could claim to be induced, the AICTE, 'made no such complaint,' and therefore 'it was not for others to insinuate that the AICTE was dishonestly induced to do something.'
policy_considerations: The court emphasized the legislative intent that inherent powers should not be used to circumvent specific statutory remedies. The court concluded that 'when there is a specific remedy provided by way of appeal or revision the inherent power under Section 482 CrPC... cannot and should not be resorted to,' ensuring that the structured procedural framework of the Code is respected.
